The Band-tailed manakin (Pipra fasciicauda) is a small passerine bird inhabiting humid lowland forests of the Amazon basin. Neonates emerge from eggs incubated at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], and field observations indicate that hatching occurs after approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days] of continuous brooding by the female. At the moment of hatching, chicks weigh a mere 1.8 grams [Wwb = 1.8 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of most suboscine passerines. This initial mass is less than twelve percent of the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which reaches 15.9 grams [Wwi = 15.9 grams], though individual variation in adult mass — from 11.5 to 19 grams — suggests considerable plasticity linked to local fruit abundance during the pre-breeding period. The onset of independent locomotion and first flight, termed fledging, occurs relatively early in development; under thermal conditions characteristic of the active metabolic phase in this species, sustained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledglings leave the nest after 16 days since birth [tx = 16 days since birth]. This brief nestling period is consistent with the intense predation pressure typical of understory nesting birds.

Puberty, defined by the completion of gonadal maturation and the onset of spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females, occurs at a remarkably consistent age when individuals are maintained under stable thermal regimes. At an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which corresponds to the species' preferred metabolic window during the breeding season, young manakins reach sexual maturity after 48 days since birth [tp = 48 days since birth]. This rapid maturation compared to other members of the Pipridae family likely reflects the selective advantage of early territory acquisition in a lekking mating system, where成年 males must establish display perches to attract females. In captivity, individuals subjected to food supplementation achieve puberty at the lower bound of this range, whereas those exposed to nutritional stress may delay maturation, although the mean value remains robust at 48 days from hatching. The energetic demands of gonadal growth are partially offset by the high metabolic rate characteristic of this species during its reproductive period, as indicated by respirometry trials conducted at the same temperature.

Respirometry measurements of basal oxygen consumption reveal a peak metabolic rate of 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when birds are resting in postabsorptive state at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value, obtained from adult males during the height of the breeding season, is among the highest recorded for a passerine of 15.9 grams [Wwi = 15.9 grams], underscoring the elevated energetic costs associated with the vigorous and frequently repeated courtship displays that characterize manakin leks. The metabolic scope between resting and displaying individuals is substantial, as males engage in acrobatic flights and wing-snapping maneuvers that can triple oxygen consumption over short intervals. Such a high basal rate also implies substantial daily energetic requirements for maintenance, which are met through a diet consisting almost exclusively of lipid-rich fruits. Comparative data from congeneric species, such as Pipra erythrocephala, suggest that this metabolic profile is an evolutionary adaptation to the energy-intensive lekking behavior that has driven sexual selection in the genus.

Reproductive output in Pipra fasciicauda is modest but consistent across years. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically initiate two nesting attempts per breeding season [F_R_i = two nesting attempts per breeding season], each requiring construction of a new nest. Given that the breeding season in Amazonian populations spans roughly six months, this yields a maximum annual reproductive rate of two eggs per year when conditions are favorable at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The limitation to a single egg per clutch is unusual among tropical passerines and may be linked to the female's need to incubate and provision a rapidly growing altricial nestling without male assistance; males contribute only to territorial defense and display. First reproduction typically occurs at 438 days since birth [tR = 438 days since birth], a value computed from the seasonal timing of lek establishment in young males and the onset of ovulation in yearling females at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay of more than a year after fledging allows juveniles to accumulate sufficient body reserves and to learn the complex display routines necessary for successful mating.

Longevity records for Band-tailed manakin under natural conditions indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 9.5 years [am = approximately 9.5 years] when individuals experience the typical thermal regime of their understory habitat, maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during active periods. This relatively extended lifespan, unusual for a 15.9-gram bird, is consistent with the slow life-history strategy implied by a single-egg clutch and a delayed age at first reproduction. Annual adult survival is estimated at over seventy percent in undisturbed forests, where predation risk from raptors and snakes remains moderate. The trade-off between current reproductive effort and future survival is evident in the species' apparent reluctance to double-brood when nest failure occurs late in the season, suggesting that individuals prioritize self-maintenance over maximal annual fecundity. Senescence in captive individuals becomes noticeable after eight years, with reduced muscle mass and diminished display vigor preceding mortality from physiological deterioration rather than extrinsic causes.
